'''Henry Edgar Hall''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (1928 – 4 December 2015) was a [[professor]] of [[low temperature physics]] at the [[University of Manchester]]. He was the 2004 recipient of the [[Guthrie Medal and Prize]]. Hall was awarded a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in 1957 from [[Emmanuel College, Cambridge]] with thesis title ''The rotation of liquid [[helium II]]''. He worked at the University of Manchester from 1958 to 1995, when he retired.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.condmat.physics.manchester.ac.uk/history/ | title = History of the Condensed Matter Physics Group | publisher = University of Manchester | access-date = 9 January 2013}}</ref> He died on 4 December 2015.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theboltonnews.co.uk/announcements/deaths/deaths/14129993.Prof__Henry_Edgar_Hall_F_R_S/|title=Prof. Henry Edgar Hall F.R.S|work=The Bolton News}}</ref><ref name=frs>Golov, A. I.; Vinen W. F. (2018). "Henry Edgar Hall. 28 September 1928—4 December 2015". ''[[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]]''. [[doi:10.1098/rsbm.2018.0020]].</ref>

==Biography==

Hall was born in London on 28 September 1928, the son of John Ainger Hall and Elsie (née Chatterton). He attended Lowther Primary School in [[Barnes, London|Barnes]] until he was nine, when he moved to the preparatory department at [[Latymer Upper School]] in [[Hammersmith & Fulham|Hammersmith]]. He remained there until he was called up for National Service with the Royal Air Force, serving in Egypt as an electrician. In his last year at school, Hall won an Open Major Scholarship to [[Emmanuel College, Cambridge]]. He went up to Emmanuel in 1949 to read natural sciences, and graduated with first class honours.

He was then accepted as a research student in the Royal Society Mond Laboratory, an offshoot of the [[Cavendish Laboratory]] where he chose to work on liquid helium, under the supervision, initially, of Donald Osborne and later, [[David Shoenberg]]. While waiting for equipment to be built, he wrote a paper explaining some apparently puzzling observations by [[Pyotr Kapitsa|Kapitsa]] of the force acting on a source of heat in superfluid helium.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hall|first=H E|title=The Inertia of Heat Flow in Liquid Helium II|journal=Proceedings of the Physical Society. Section A|volume=67|issue=6|pages=485–494|date=1954|doi=10.1088/0370-1298/67/6/301|bibcode=1954PPSA...67..485H}}</ref> The initial experimental results were published in 1955.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hall|first1=H E|last2=Vinen|first2=W F|title=LXIV. Non-linear dissipative processes in liquid helium 11|journal=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science|volume=46|issue=376|pages=546–548|date=1955|doi=10.1080/14786440508520591}}</ref> The background to this complex field is fully described in the Royal Society biographical memoir.<ref name=frs/>

In 1958 Hall was appointed to a lectureship at the [[University of Manchester]], where he remained for the rest of his career. He collaborated with A J F Boyle, D St P Bunbury and others in studies of the newly discovered [[Mössbauer effect]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last2=Hall|first2=H E|last1=Boyle|first1=A J F|title=The Mössbauer effect|journal=Reports on Progress in Physics|volume=25|pages=441–524|date=1962|issue=1|doi=10.1088/0034-4885/25/1/311|bibcode=1962RPPh...25..441B|s2cid=250915692 }}</ref> In 1961 Hall was promoted directly to a professorship. He went on to play an important role in the development of [[dilution refrigerator]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hall|first1=H E|last2=Ford|first2=P J|last3=Thompson|first3=K|title=A helium-3 dilution refrigerator|journal=Cryogenics|volume=6|issue=2|pages=80–88|date=April 1966|doi=10.1016/0011-2275(66)90034-8|bibcode=1966Cryo....6...80H}}</ref> His growing expertise in experiments at very low temperatures led him to studies of the liquid phase of the light isotope of helium, <sup>3</sup>He, especially in its superfluid state.

Hall retired in 1995, but continued his research full time until 2000. He ran experiments on non-linear mass currents in <sup>3</sup>He-B at near-critical velocities—calling that period ‘my second graduate studies’.<ref name=frs/> He summarized the results in his paper of 2001.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hall|first1=H E|title=Nonlinear Dynamics of Superflow in 3He-B: The Coupling of Sound and Helmholtz Oscillations|journal=Journal of Low Temperature Physics|volume=124|issue=5/6|pages=537–572|date=2001|doi=10.1023/A:1012269828925|s2cid=118165530}}</ref>

===Family===

Hall married physics student Patricia Broadbent in 1962. They had two sons, Stephan and Ian, and a daughter, Daphne.

Henry Edgar Hall died on 4 December 2015 in Millview Care Home, [[Bolton]].<ref>{{Cite news|title=Death Notices & Obituaries: Prof. Henry Edgar Hall FRS|newspaper= The Bolton News|date=8 December 2015}}</ref>

==Awards==

1963 [[Simon Memorial Prize]], [[Institute of Physics]] (with W. F. Vinen)<br />2004 [[Institute of Physics Michael Faraday Medal and Prize|Guthrie Medal and Prize]], Institute of Physics
